passages.t: ‘Great is the LORD’ in the city of our God, and ‘tell the next generation’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A song. A Psalm of the sons of Korah” (verse 1). It praises God in his city. “Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised in the city of our God, His holy mountain” (verse 1). Zion is “the joy of all the earth” (verse 2). “God is in her citadels; He has shown Himself to be a fortress” (verse 3).

Then a short story. Kings gathered against the city. “They saw and were astounded; they fled in terror” (verse 5). God broke their pride as an east wind smashes ships (verse 7).

Inside the temple the people think about God's love. “Within Your temple, O God, we contemplate Your loving devotion” (verse 9).

The psalm ends with a walk. “March around Zion, encircle her, count her towers, consider her ramparts, tour her citadels, that you may tell the next generation” (verses 12 and 13). Why? “For this God is our God forever and ever; He will be our guide even till death” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Verse 2 says Zion is “like the peaks of Zaphon”. Zaphon was the name of a high mountain far to the north, in Syria. In the old texts of the city of Ugarit it was the home of the storm god Baal. Zion is a modest hill. To call it Zaphon was a bold claim: the true mountain of God is not Baal's peak but the place where the LORD lives.

The ‘ships of Tarshish’ were large ships built for long trading voyages. They stood for wealth and human power. Isaiah names them among the proud things God will bring low (Isaiah 2:16).

The kings who fled are not named. Some readers think of the Assyrian siege that failed. Others think the psalm celebrates God's care in general words. Psalms 46, 47 and 48 sit together as songs of Zion.
passages.later:
Jesus called Jerusalem “the city of the great King” (Matthew 5:35), using the words of verse 2.

The New Testament carries Zion's hope beyond the earthly city. “Instead, you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22).
passages.hard: The psalm says God will establish the city forever, yet Jerusalem was later destroyed more than once. Was it wrong? Before the exile some people did treat the temple as a lucky charm. Jeremiah warned them, “Do not trust in deceptive words, chanting: ‘This is the temple of the LORD’” (Jeremiah 7:4). But the psalm itself rests its hope on God's presence and his loving devotion, not on stones. Notice its last line: ‘this God’, not ‘these walls’. As the note on Psalm 46 says, this is not a promise about any modern city or state.
passages.asks:
Why count the towers? So that you can ‘tell the next generation’. Faith is something you look at closely, so that you can pass it on.

Who is your next generation? A child, a younger friend, someone new to faith. What has God done that you could walk them round and show them?
